title: 'Gone in a Blink': Nepal Floods Sweep Away Indian Migrant Workers
excerpt: Survivors Neyaz Miya and Mehadi Hassan watched the Syafrubesi hotels they had helped build disappear on August 26; three colleagues from their Bihar village remain missing.
body:
• Flash floods on August 26 wiped out Syafrubesi, a market town in Nepal's Rasuwa district near the Tibet border.
  • More than 1,200 bodies have been recovered, at least 4,000 people remain missing and more than 13,000 have been rescued, according to reports.
  • Neyaz Miya and Mehadi Hassan, migrant workers from Bihar's Bettiah district, survived; three colleagues from their village remain missing.
  • The disaster struck a corridor that depends on Indian migrant labour — 97 percent of Nepal's foreign-born residents are from India.

Gone in a blink

BETTIAH, India: Neyaz Miya was adjusting a kitchen handle. Mehadi Hassan was fixing a bracket for a bed. They were at different construction sites — Miya in a half-constructed home higher up the hill, Hassan on the ground floor of Ganesh Hotel, closer to the Trishuli River that flows through Syafrubesi — when the water came.

"First came the terrifying loud sound. Then the ground trembled, and dark clouds descended upon us," recalled Miya, 34, who ran further up the hill with his phone and slippers, five or six others running alongside him. Hassan, lower on the slope, did not wait for slippers or phone. He just ran, climbing a narrow stair-like path until he reached roughly 60 metres above the road.

From that height, the two men watched the town they had helped build disappear. The multi-storey hotels whose interiors they had fitted over a decade were swallowed; Syafrubesi, a market town near the Nepal-Tibet border of 2,271 people in the 2011 census, was gone.

"The town was gone in a blink. There were only three kinds of people who survived that day: those who were out of town, those who were at work and managed to run, and those who lived a little higher up the hill."

— Neyaz Miya, survivor

Context & Background

The August 26 floods were triggered by a massive collapse of glacial ice and rock in the Himalayas, possibly set off by a magnitude-4.4 seismic event. The USGS later said the seismic signal was the collapse itself — a wall of water, mud and boulders, some 25 feet across, thundering down the valley. Rescue operations have been hampered by destroyed roads, power outages and broken communications.

The 216-megawatt Upper Trishuli 1 hydropower project was dashed to pieces after an early-warning system failed again; of roughly 1,400 workers on site, more than 500 are missing. Reuters reported that two men survived nine days trapped in a flood tunnel, sheltering in an air pocket just 160 metres from the exit. More than 7,500 houses across the valley have been destroyed.

Impact & Analysis

That morning, Miya and Hassan had left for work with 34-year-old Arman Ansari, 20-year-old Samir Ansari and 52-year-old Mukhtar Ansari, all from their Turhapatti village. Arman was working beside Hassan on the ground floor; Samir and Mukhtar were on the top floor of the Full Moon Hotel. When Hassan ran up the hill, he believed Arman was behind him. The other three were never seen again.

Arman's 14-year-old son Salman Alam and his friend Shibu Alam, 17, had come to visit the hills a month earlier and made it up the hill with Miya and Hassan. "Salman was crying, howling and searching for his father," Hassan said. Weeks on, the boy still cannot sleep: "The moment I close my eyes, I feel the flood is coming for me."

Arman's wife, Sahrun Khatun, has only her last phone call with her husband to hold on to — two hours before the floods. Mukhtar's son Osama, a tailor in Kathmandu, has submitted his DNA samples. The three families are preparing to host a bhoj, the funeral feast — having given up on hope.

Diaspora Angle

Turhapatti is among thousands of villages along the 1,715-km India-Nepal border, where generations have crossed back and forth in search of work. The bond is known as roti-beti ka rishta — a relationship of food and daughters — and per Nepal's 2021 census, the country had 700,000 foreign-born residents, 97 percent of them from India.

A carpenter or mason earns 600-700 rupees a day on the Indian side, about 900 rupees for the same work in Nepal. Miya, who owns only 0.03 hectares, had been sending 30,000 rupees a month to his family of ten; Hassan, who inherited a 6x8-metre room and no land, sent 15,000. For diaspora families with roots in Bihar and eastern UP, these are the households behind the remittance economy — and the floods have cut their lifelines.

What's Next

Rescue and recovery operations continue across the valley, though hopes of finding more survivors are fading. The two survivors, Miya and Hassan, are already making calls to find work again — this time in Nepal's plains. They pledge never to return to the hills. "My whole body shivers at the thought of going there," says Hassan.
nri_angle: The disaster struck the open-border migration corridor between India and Nepal, where lakhs of Indian workers earn their families' livelihoods — a story that lands directly with the diaspora and their families back home.
author: Diaspora Desk
